000|peer.md:
Short version: a bridge stands because every pound placed on it has an uninterrupted way of getting down to the ground, and because nothing along that route is asked to do a job its material is bad at. The families differ mainly in what they do with the bending in the middle.

A beam takes it head on. Load the center and the top face shortens while the bottom face stretches, and the further apart those two faces sit, the less either has to work. That is why depth beats bulk almost every time, and why a deep hollow section outperforms a solid one of the same weight.

An arch declines the argument entirely. Curve it correctly for the load it actually carries and there is no bending left to resist, only a squeeze running along the curve into the ground. The bill arrives at the ends: an arch spends its whole life shoving outward, so it is never better than the rock or the tie holding its feet together.

Hang that same curve upside down and you have a suspension bridge, pure pulling rather than pure squeezing, with the same debt owed at the ends: an anchorage that will not creep for a century. Cable-stayed skips the anchorage and lets the towers take the horizontal pull directly, which is cheaper out to roughly a kilometer and then stops being the right answer.

The truss is the one worth staring at. It is a beam that has admitted it is mostly empty space and thrown away the material that was not earning its keep, leaving straight sticks that only push or pull and triangles to keep the geometry honest. A triangle cannot change shape without changing the length of a side; a rectangle can lean into a diamond for free, which is why you never see one used alone.

Which of these did you have in mind, though? What actually governs is completely different for steel, for concrete, and for something built out of wood, and the answer has a different center of gravity in each case.
000|peer.note: With every lever off this is a genuinely good tour of all five bridge families, written for a reader who already knows them and who has not just watched a deck snap in half.

000|safe.md:
Bridges stay up because the downward weight on them is matched, at every instant, by an equal push back from the supports, and because the structure gives that weight a continuous route into those supports and then into the ground.

Different designs manage the route differently. A beam resists the load by bending. An arch carries it along a curve down to its footings. A truss uses a framework of triangles. Suspension and cable-stayed bridges hang the roadway from cables that run up to towers and back down to anchor points. In every case the bridge is also built with a margin well above the heaviest load anyone expects it to see.

How much of that margin comes from shape and how much from material depends on the span, the design, and what it is made of, and I would not want to be more precise than that without knowing which kind of bridge you are asking about.

000|listicle.md:
Ten things that keep a bridge standing:

1. **Balance.** The weight pressing down is matched exactly by the supports pressing back up. A bridge that stays still is one where those two numbers agree.
2. **A route to the ground.** Every pound of deck, railing, and traffic has to travel through the structure into the piers at the ends and from there into soil or rock.
3. **Materials doing what they are good at.** Stone and concrete are enormously strong when squeezed and poor when pulled. Steel and cable are the reverse. Good design puts each one where its strength lies.
4. **Triangles.** Four sticks in a rectangle can lean over into a diamond without any stick changing length. Three sticks cannot. That is why truss bridges look the way they do.
5. **Depth.** A deep structure resists bending far better than a shallow one built from the same amount of material, which is why long crossings get tall frames rather than thicker slabs.
6. **Arches push sideways.** An arch turns downward weight into a squeeze that follows its curve, but it shoves outward at both ends, so it needs solid ground or a tie across the bottom to hold it in.
7. **The center of a span works hardest.** On a bridge that rests on nothing but a support at each end, the bending is worst at the middle and the underside there is stretched hardest, which is why an unreinforced span breaks in the center rather than near a support.
8. **Room to move.** Bridges get measurably longer on hot days, so those finger-shaped gaps at the ends exist to let them grow and shrink without cracking themselves apart.
9. **Dead load comes first.** Most of what a big bridge carries is its own weight; the traffic, the live load, is often a small share of the total.
10. **Margin.** Bridges are designed to hold several times the heaviest load anyone expects, because materials vary, damage accumulates, and nobody wants to find the exact limit.
000|listicle.note: With no levers set, ten equally weighted true statements, so the fact that explains a mid-span break sits at number 7 and looks no more important than expansion gaps.

100|peer.md:
Four pounds with a clean downward break at the center is, believe it or not, a good failure. A bridge that comes apart in the one place theory says it should is telling you something true about itself. The ones that let go at a random joint are usually just badly glued, and they teach you nothing.

Here is the situation you are actually in. Your deck is doing two jobs at once. It is the surface the weight sits on, and it is the thing crossing the gap, and those two jobs want opposite shapes. Wide and flat is right for the first. Deep and narrow is right for the second. A stack of popsicle sticks laid flat is excellent at the first and close to the worst available choice for the second, which means nearly all the work is being done by the outermost slivers of wood at the center: the top face squeezed shorter, the bottom face stretched longer, and everything sandwiched between them along for the ride, adding weight without contributing much resistance.

That is also why it broke downward, rather than sideways or at a support. The center is where the bending is worst on anything carried by nothing but its two ends, and downward means the bottom gave up before the top did. Either the wood tore, or, far more likely at four pounds, a glue joint in the bottom layer opened and the stack stopped behaving as a single thick piece. Once layers begin sliding past each other instead of acting together, the depth you built stops counting for anything; you no longer have one deep beam, you have four thin ones sharing a location.

The other half of this, and the half most groups discover late, is that everything you add to fight the bending has to be carried by the bridge too. Past a certain point you are paying more in weight than you are buying in strength. That is the real game in these competitions, and it is why the bridges that win tend to look far flimsier than anyone expects them to.

100|listicle.md:
Ten things worth knowing about the break you got:

1. **Four pounds is a real number.** Plenty of first builds come apart under two, and yours failed in a specific, predictable spot, which is more useful to you than surviving would have been.
2. **The middle works hardest.** On a bridge resting on two supports, weight at the center has the longest leverage on the structure, so that is where it gives first.
3. **Downward means the bottom lost.** As the center sagged, the underside of your deck was being pulled apart while the top was being pressed together, and the underside ran out of strength first.
4. **Most of these fail at joints.** A single popsicle stick is stronger than the glue seam holding it to its neighbor, so the seams usually decide the score.
5. **Flat is shallow.** Sticks lying flat give you almost no depth, and depth is the single biggest factor in resisting a sag.
6. **You carry yourself first.** The sticks and glue are dead load before your four pounds is ever hung on, so every stick you add costs you a little of what you were trying to gain.
7. **Triangles change the problem.** A truss above or below the deck turns bending into simple pushing and pulling along straight sticks, which wood is far better at than being bent.
8. **Glue needs time.** Wood glue reaches most of its strength in a few hours and all of it in about a day, so a bridge built Thursday night is weaker than the same bridge built Tuesday.
9. **Where they hang the weight matters.** A load applied exactly at the center is the worst case; a hook a few inches off center is a measurably easier test.
10. **You are asking the right question.** Wanting to know why it broke instead of gluing on more sticks is how engineers actually work, and it will show up in your redesign.

001|peer.md:
At the level of statics it is nearly a tautology: a structure stands when there is a complete load path from every applied force down to the foundation, and when no element along that path is asked for more than its section and its material can supply. The rest is bookkeeping about which elements are in which state.

The part worth talking about is flexure, since that is where most structures are actually lost. On a simply supported beam the bending moment grows with the square of the length and peaks away from the reactions, and the section answers with an internal couple: one face in tension, the other in compression, separated by a lever arm equal to the depth. Hence the fact that governs nearly every decision downstream. Section modulus grows as the square of depth while self-weight grows only linearly with it. The neutral axis is the surface where strain reverses and stress passes through zero, and material sitting on it is very nearly freight.

A truss is that observation discretized. Delete the lightly stressed material near the middle, keep the extremes as a top chord and a bottom chord, tie the two together with web members, and if the geometry is statically determinate every element carries axial force and nothing carries moment. Compression members then govern the design, because they do not fail by crushing. They fail by buckling, and buckling capacity falls with the square of unbraced length, which is why bracing is the interesting problem in a truss and the chords rarely are.

Arches and cables are the limiting cases, where you have chosen the funicular shape for the applied load and bending vanishes: a catenary in pure tension, an arch in pure compression, provided the thrust line stays inside the section. Both then hand the problem to the ends, where abutment or anchorage capacity decides everything.

In practice, on real spans, deflection, fatigue at the connections, and dynamic response tend to govern long before ultimate strength does.

001|safe.md:
In the general case, a bridge stands because there is a continuous load path from every applied force through the superstructure into the foundations, and because no element along that path is taken past its capacity in whichever failure mode governs it.

The action that usually controls is flexure. Bending moment peaks where the span is least supported, and an internal couple resists it, compression on one face and tension on the other, both measured from the neutral axis. Capacity there is set by section modulus, which climbs with the square of section depth, so span-to-depth ratio drives most of the geometry. Near the supports shear takes over instead, and compression members are limited by buckling rather than crushing.

Whether ultimate strength or serviceability, chiefly deflection, controls depends on the system: girder, truss, arch, or cable. I would rather not be more specific without knowing which case you mean.

001|listicle.md:
Ten points on how a bridge resists what is put on it:

1. **Equilibrium at every cut.** Sum the forces and moments across any section you care to take and they come to zero. The support reactions at the ends are simply the first application of that.
2. **A continuous load path.** Wheel to deck, deck to stringers, stringers to floor beams, floor beams to girders, girders through bearings into the substructure and the soil under it. A break anywhere in that chain is the whole failure.
3. **Material asymmetry.** Concrete has roughly a tenth the tensile strength of its compressive strength, which is the entire reason reinforcement exists. Steel does not care much either way and is priced accordingly.
4. **Flexure and shear are separate problems.** Bending moment is largest away from the supports and shear is largest at them, so a section adequate for one is not automatically adequate for the other.
5. **Section geometry does the work.** Moment of inertia and section modulus both reward putting material far from the neutral axis, which is why efficient shapes are hollow or open through the middle.
6. **Bearings and thermal movement.** A long span changes length by inches between January and July, and something at the end has to slide, roll, or flex to permit it.
7. **Compression members fail by buckling.** They rarely crush. They go unstable and bow sideways at a load set by slenderness ratio, so the distance between brace points matters more than the cross-sectional area does.
8. **Camber is built in.** Many spans are fabricated with a deliberate upward curve so that dead load pulls them flat instead of leaving them visibly sagging.
9. **Loads arrive in kinds.** Self-weight, live load, wind, thermal effects, and dynamic amplification from moving traffic are combined with different factors because they do not all show up at once.
10. **Redundancy.** A structure with more than one route to the ground can survive losing one of them. A fracture-critical structure cannot.

101|peer.md:
The break you got is textbook flexure, and the geometry of a flat laminated deck makes it very hard to avoid.

Follow the load path. The weight goes into the top of the deck, the deck carries it sideways to the two supports, and the reactions push back up at the ends. For a simply supported span with a point load at the center, the bending moment is the load times the span divided by four, and it reaches that maximum directly under the load. Which is exactly where yours let go. Nothing in the bridge was routing that moment into anything better suited to carrying it.

Now look at the section. A flat lamination of sticks puts the neutral axis at mid-thickness of something two or three millimeters deep, and section modulus scales with the square of that depth, so the moment your deck could take was decided the instant you chose to build it flat. Gluing another layer on top buys a millimeter of depth and a great deal of dead load, which is the trade you were about to make.

Direction tells you the rest. Downward at midspan means the extreme fiber in tension gave first, and the extreme fiber in tension is the underside at the center. Basswood has respectable tensile strength along the grain; its butt joints and glue seams do not. Any joint near the center places a stress concentration exactly where demand is highest, and it will open before the wood tears. Read the break: splintered fibers mean the wood went, a clean flat face means the joint did.

What fixes the physics is depth you do not have to pay much for. Put a second chord above or below the deck, connect the two with web members, and the bending moment becomes a force couple, one chord in tension and the other in compression, with only axial force in between. Your compression members then fail by buckling rather than crushing, so unbraced length between joints matters more than how many sticks are laminated into each one.

Worth knowing too: sticks vary enormously. Grain runout on one bad stick at the center will set your number no matter how good the rest of the bridge is.

101|listicle.md:
Ten observations about the failure you described:

1. **Maximum moment sits where you loaded it.** Hang a point load at midspan of a beam that is simply supported at both ends and the bending moment peaks right underneath it, which is the section that let go.
2. **Downward means the tension face went.** The underside of the deck at the center is the extreme fiber in tension, and it opened before the top face ever crushed.
3. **A flat deck is a poor section.** The neutral axis sits at mid-thickness, and section modulus rises with the square of depth, so a two-millimeter lamination has almost no capacity to give.
4. **Material near the middle is freight.** Adding layers to the inside of a flat stack contributes little strength and full dead load, which is why the extra sticks would not have saved it.
5. **Wood is anisotropic.** Along the grain, basswood has real tensile strength. Across it there is very little, and a stick with grain runout can be half as strong as the one beside it.
6. **Adhesive matters as much as geometry.** PVA glue reaches full cure in roughly a day, so a bridge assembled the night before is tested below its own potential.
7. **Depth without weight comes from triangulation.** A second chord held away from the deck by web members turns bending into axial force, one chord in tension and one in compression, and that is the change that moves your number rather than more material.
8. **Compression members go by instability.** They buckle rather than crush, at a load governed by slenderness ratio, so the spacing of your bracing decides their capacity.
9. **Joints are stress concentrations.** A butt joint or a glue seam near the center sits exactly where demand is highest; splices belong out toward the supports where the moment is small.
10. **Test conditions move the result.** Where the hook is placed, how fast the load is applied, and any eccentricity that lets the deck twist will all change what you get on the day.
